name: Parc de Bagatelle

beats.script_body: The small château at the heart of the Parc de Bagatelle was built on a wager. In September 1777, the Comte d'Artois — brother of Louis XVI and the future Charles X — bet his sister-in-law Queen Marie-Antoinette that he could erect a fully habitable residence on the Bagatelle site within the roughly sixty days of the court's annual stay at Fontainebleau, in time to host a grand reception on their return. He engaged the neoclassical architect François-Joseph Bélanger and put nearly nine hundred workers on the site day and night. He won the bet, completing the house in sixty-three days. The source text identifies this building as being built by 'the brother of Louis XVI, the future Charles X' — consistent with the Comte d'Artois.

beats.script_body: In late May, over a thousand varieties of roses bloom in the Rose Garden of the Parc de Bagatelle, creating a vast canvas of pastels and bold reds between the Seine and a small hill topped by a pagoda. Among the famous women of Paris who reveled in roses were the legendary mistresses of Louis XV — Madame de Pompadour, for whom flowers, specifically roses, were one of the passions of her life, and her successor Madame du Barry, of whom the king said she was 'the only woman in France who can make me forget that I am in my sixties.' Empress Joséphine, wife of Napoleon, and later the chaste Empress Eugénie, wife of Napoleon III, both cherished roses as emblems of romantic love.

As you walk the perfumed paths of the rosaires and read the poetic names affixed to each bush—'Daydream,' a hot pink—you may enjoy the cultural associations of the garden. Among the famous women of Paris who reveled in roses were the legendary mistresses of Louis XV, Madame de Pompadour (flowers—specifically, roses—were one of the passions of her life), and her successor, Madame du Barry—'the only woman in France who can make me forget that I am in my sixties,' said the king. Empress Joséphine, the wife of Napoleon, and later the chaste Empress Eugénie, wife of Napoleon's nephew, Napoleon III, who, like his uncle, reigned as self-declared emperor, also preferred roses to all other flowers: both cherished them as emblems of romantic love.

beats.script_body: The Bois — or woodlands — that surround the Bagatelle originally served as a royal hunting ground and a 'discreetly leafy' romantic hideout, to quote historian Alistair Horne. The 2,200 acres of beech, linden, cedar, chestnuts, elm, and fifteen thousand mulberry trees include remnants of the ancient Forêt de Rouvray, to which Haussmann and Alphand gave a more designed landscape in the nineteenth century. But always this bucolic getaway on the western edge of Paris — where fashionable people, women in their carriages and men on horseback, went to see and to be seen — offered opportunities for hedonistic orgies and secret sexual encounters.

beats.script_body: In 1846, during the fireworks of the sixteenth anniversary of the 1830 Citizens Revolution, Gustave Flaubert and his lover, the poet Louise Colet — one of the models for Emma Bovary — took a long hansom cab ride through the Bois de Boulogne. According to Colet's biographer, their coach moved slowly amid a raging lightning storm and bursts of flashing rockets, patriotic shouting, and thunder deafening throughout Paris, as 'flashes of lightning seem to celebrate their lust.' As Flaubert wrote to Colet a few days later: 'They blazed for us . . . like a flaming beginning of love.' Jean-Paul Sartre was certain that Louise's and Gustave's first lovemaking took place then and there, inside that black hansom cab.

beats.script_body: Marcel Proust, who played in the Bois as a child, resurrected it in Swann's Way. The fashionable courtesans of Colette's Chéri staged their promenades and liaisons érotiques in the shelter of the ancient trees, their spirited rendezvous the backdrop of the opening scene of the film Gigi. Director Robert Bresson takes a more satiric view of the women of western Paris in his 1945 film Les Dames du Bois de Boulogne. The 2001 novel The Sexual Life of Catherine M, by Catherine Millet, describes the nightlife of prostitutes and groupies in the area of the Porte Dauphine entrance, northeast of the gardens — descriptions not taken as fictional.

beats.script_body: Here on the hillside of once rural Passy, the writer Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850), whose finances were as complicated as the plots of his novels, evaded his creditors and escaped out the back door down into rue Berton when they caught up with him. The walk up the hill from the Passy metro station, 'hidden behind chestnut trees and roses, and the tracks leading towards the Pont de Bir-Hakeim . . . famous from Last Tango in Paris,' leads to rue Raynouard and, after a five-minute walk, to the entrance to Balzac's cottage. Once you descend into the garden you feel as if you've left far behind the city and the monotonous suburb, the sixteenth arrondissement — 'snob Passy' to the protagonist of Alan Furst's novel of Occupied Paris, Red Gold.

beats.script_body: As the self-defined 'secretary of French society,' Balzac wrote almost one hundred novels here, a chronicle entitled La Comédie Humaine — The Human Comedy. He began writing at midnight, continued until midday, fueled by black coffee. Because he didn't limit — or patronize — his readers with his 'judgmental interference,' an admiring Henry James preferred him to Flaubert. Nowadays, to quote Francine Prose, when readers and publishers demand happy endings and 'sympathetic' characters, 'few novelists would have the nerve' to produce Balzac's brand of unsparing, courageous fiction in which the faces of Paris blend corruption, misery, vanity, and glory.

beats.script_body: The dying Cousin Bette 'kept the Secret of her hate' from the family she'd tried to destroy, who in their ignorance mourned her 'as the angel of the family.' When Bette's cousin asks what is the cause of the deep-rooted evil in the world, Balzac's answer is a want of religion and the 'encroachment of money . . . another name for egoism solidified. Money has become the measure of everything.' Cousin Bette (1846) is one of the masterpieces Balzac wrote here, at his cottage in Passy.

name: Allée des Cygnes

beats.script_body: En route to Passy, get off the elevated number 6 metro at Bir-Hakeim — named for a French victory in North Africa in 1942 — then walk halfway across the lower level of the double metro and road bridge until you reach the stairway on the left. It leads down to this quiet, mesmerising walk across a narrow man-made island in the Seine, lined with plane trees and benches from which you can look up at the exquisite gray grillwork on the top level of the bridge and the sculpted green river gods on the bottom. This was a favorite walk of Samuel Beckett.

short_description: Elevated terrace and gardens facing the Eiffel Tower across the Seine, built around the 1937 Palais de Chaillot

beats.script_body: By some accounts Trocadéro is a monumentally ugly stone heap facing the Eiffel Tower, and by others it is 'the prettiest spot in Paris.' The hill of Chaillot — the historic name of the place — offers a view over the Seine just where the river swings south-westwards, 'unequaled by any other.' The gardens, with jet fountains, pine trees, flowers, and meticulously groomed hedges, slope down to the Seine, and at sunset the dome of Les Invalides in the distance glows like liquid gold. A bronze sculpture of Benjamin Franklin, Passy resident, at the end of rue Benjamin Franklin injects a kindly American presence on the Place. Ambassador Franklin was happy in Paris: he was 'among a people that love me, and whom I love.'

beats.script_body: Renovated in 1999, the Parc des Serres d'Auteuil at 3 avenue de la Porte d'Auteuil is one of the most magnificent garden structures in Europe, made of metal and glass and greenery. There is a rare silence here, though the innovative green space is popular with Parisians.

beats.source_passage: PARC des serres d'auteuil 3, avenue de la Porte d'Auteuil. Metro, Porte d'Auteuil (10—7, according to the season). Renovated, in 1999, this is one of the most magnificent garden structures in Europe, made of metal and glass and greenery. There is a rare silence here, though the innovative green space is popular with Parisians.

flagged_claims.note: Confirmed: the grand palmarium at the Jardin des Serres d'Auteuil was completely renovated in 1999. Sources: https://www.paris.fr/lieux/jardin-des-serres-d-auteuil-1780

opening_hours_basis: A fenced botanical garden and greenhouse complex with closing gates; gated, hours not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Botanical garden with historic glasshouses; strolling the ornamental grounds takes about twenty minutes and the greenhouses of tropical and palm collections add roughly half an hour walking through them.
judgement_basis: This botanical garden with greenhouses has traffic-free outdoor lawns and paths where children can run and free benches quiet enough to talk, but glasshouse interiors expect care and the whole enclosure is gated and locked at night so it fails after dark.
queue_basis: This botanical greenhouse garden has open park access but a controlled entrance to the historic glasshouses, producing only a short desk or bag-check line at peak midday.
